reasoning_summary: The proof forms G = (V, M u M') for two perfect matchings M, M' of a tree T. Every vertex is covered exactly once by each matching, so deg_G(v) is 1 (both matchings use the same edge at v) or 2 (they use different edges); hence every component of G is a path or a cycle. A path component of length >= 2 is impossible: if an endpoint v has degree 1, its unique incident edge vu lies in both M and M', so u is matched to v by both matchings and also has degree 1. Therefore every component is either a single edge lying in M n M' or a cycle. G is a subgraph of the acyclic T, so no cycle component can occur, forcing every edge of M u M' to lie in M n M', i.e. M = M'. I tried to build a counterexample by looking for a tree, two perfect matchings, and a component of M u M' that is a path of length >= 2 (which would break the case split), and the degree argument above rules it out; I also checked small trees (P2, P4, P6, the spider on 6 vertices) where the union always splits into shared edges only. The one real defect is wording: line 0006 calls the first case an 'isolated vertex' when the component is actually a single edge belonging to both matchings (for T = P4 with M = M' = {ab, cd}, the components of G are the edges ab and cd, not isolated vertices). The parenthetical 'which is in M and M'' shows the intended meaning, and the conclusion drawn from that case (the edge lies in both matchings) is exactly what the final step uses, so the argument is sound; the omitted justification of the case split is standard and true. Terminological slip, not a mathematical error.
